q.intro.text: A one-mile relay is split equally among six runners. Each runs one sixth of a mile.

q.calc.text: Your calculator shows one divided by six equals zero point one six six six six six six six six seven.

q.ask.text: Which of these is exactly one sixth?

e.intro.text: Four steps. Press each one: the picture moves first, then the notation.

e.s1.text: One sixth means one divided by six. Six does not fit into one: digit zero, remainder one. Bring down a zero: ten divided by six is one, remainder four.

e.s2.text: Remainder four becomes forty. Forty divided by six is six, remainder four. The remainder four is back.

e.s3.text: Same remainder, same next line, forever: the six repeats. Only the six, because the one came once. So one sixth is zero point one six, with the six repeating.

e.s4.text: Times one hundred moves the point two places: sixteen point six six six percent. Read the block again from the new point: one sixth is sixteen point six repeating percent, exactly.

e.why.text: Quick check: why does the bar go over the six only?

e.w-ok.text: Yes. The one came from remainder one, which never comes back. Remainder four keeps coming back, and it always makes a six.

e.w-all.text: A bar over one six would mean zero point one six one six one six, and so on. But the one comes only once.

e.w-last.text: The bar is not about the last digit you wrote. It covers the block that repeats, here just the six.

t.intro.text: Now twelve runners share a five-mile relay: five twelfths of a mile each. The first step is done for you.

t.given.text: Five divided by twelve is zero, remainder five. Then fifty divided by twelve is four, remainder two. Then twenty divided by twelve is one, remainder eight.

t.step.text: Your step: the remainder eight becomes eighty. What is eighty divided by twelve?

t.s-ok.text: Yes: six times twelve is seventy-two, and eighty minus seventy-two is eight. Remainder eight again!

t.s-big.text: Seven times twelve is eighty-four, more than eighty. Try one less.

t.s-rem.text: A remainder must be less than twelve. Check: the digit times twelve, then eighty minus that.

t.s-other.text: How many twelves fit into eighty? Then eighty minus that is the remainder.

t.write.text: Remainder eight came back. Which is five twelfths in bar notation?

t.w-ok.text: Yes: remainder eight keeps coming back and makes a six every time. The four and the one came once. Five twelfths is zero point four one six, with the six repeating.

t.w-all.text: That repeats four one six again and again. The four and the one came once; only the six repeats.

t.w-two.text: A bar over one six repeats the one and the six. The one came once; only the six repeats.

t.w-stop.text: Zero point four one six stops. The remainder is eight, not zero, so the sixes go on.

t.pct.text: Last step: write five twelfths as an exact percent.

t.p-ok.text: Yes: times one hundred gives forty-one point six six six percent, and the six still repeats.

t.p-unscaled.text: That would be less than one percent. Multiply by one hundred first.

t.p-one.text: Times one hundred moves the point two places, not one.

t.p-drop.text: Forty-one point six percent stops. After the shift the sixes still go on, so the bar stays.

t.cb-right.text: At the start you picked zero point one six with the six repeating, and you were right. Now you know where the bar comes from: a remainder that comes back.

t.cb-calc.text: At the start you picked the calculator's answer. The display ran out of room: one sixth never stops.

t.cb-all.text: At the start you picked a bar over one six. That repeats the one too, but the one comes once.

t.cb-none.text: At the start: one sixth is zero point one six with the six repeating, exactly. The calculator only shows the first ten digits.

p.intro.text: Ava says one third equals zero point three three three, exactly. Is Ava right?

p.test.text: Let's test it. Build the argument and see where it leads.

p.prove.text: Now prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.c1.text: After three digits, one divided by three still has a remainder of one, not zero, because ten divided by three is three, remainder one, at every step.

p.c2.text: so three times zero point three three three is zero point nine nine nine: that is one thousandth short of one, because that leftover thousandth was never shared out.

p.c3.text: so one third is zero point three repeating, exactly, and zero point three three three is only close to one third, because cutting a repeating decimal off gives a different, smaller number.

p.x-length.text: Three threes are just three digits, and then it stops. Repeating means it goes on forever, which is what a bar says.

p.x-ends.text: It never does: every step is ten divided by three, three, remainder one. The remainder one comes back forever.

p.x-inexact.text: Some decimals are exact: zero point one two five is exactly one eighth. The question is whether zero point three three three is all of one third. It is not.

p.x-other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line.

p.done.text: That's a proof: three claims, each with its reason, and the division backs every one. Ava's number is close to one third; exactly, one third is zero point three repeating.
